links.effect: Strong discrimination persisted (c=0.868 UPMC, 0.827 VHA); calibration improved slightly after recalibration, mainly at extremes, little change near frailty threshold.
links.quote: The RAI scoring system remains robust after a decade of widespread use without evidence of meaningful algorithmic drift.

links.effect: One additional frail reclassification required screening 1400-6000 patients with the recalibrated system, depending on threshold score.
links.quote: Decision curve analysis demonstrated that reclassification of just a single additional patient as frail would require screening 1400-6000 patients with the recalibrated system, depending on the threshold score defining frailty, and after accounting for the harms of false-positive classification, weighted proportional to the odds at each threshold probability.

links.effect: Calibration improved slightly after recalibration; the model tended to underpredict mortality at extremes, with little change around the frailty threshold.
links.quote: Calibration improved slightly, especially at the extremes where the model tends to underpredict mortality, but little change was observed in the range around the threshold of frailty.

links.effect: Existing RAI-C discrimination was higher at UPMC than VHA: c = 0.868 95% CI [0.864-0.872] versus 0.827 [0.822-0.832].
links.quote: In 410,715 patients from UPMC and 190,044 patients from VHA, the existing RAI-C scoring system demonstrated strong discrimination (c = 0.868 95% CI [0.864-0.872] for UPMC, 0.827 [0.822-0.832] for VHA) which improved modestly after recalibrating parameter weights (c = 0.872 95% CI [0.868-0.876], for UPMC, 0.839 [0.834-0.845] for VHA).

links.effect: After a decade, no meaningful algorithmic drift; existing RAI-C discrimination c = 0.868 95% CI [0.864-0.872] at UPMC and 0.827 [0.822-0.832] at VHA.
links.quote: The RAI scoring system remains robust after a decade of widespread use without evidence of meaningful algorithmic drift.
